readingInstruction: Read Psalm 2. It is one of the royal psalms, quoted again and again in the New Testament. Read it as four scenes: the nations rebel (vv. 1-3), God laughs (vv. 4-6), the Son speaks (vv. 7-9), and the kings are warned (vv. 10-12).
settingTheScene: Psalm 2 was probably used at the coronation of a king in David’s line, when surrounding nations might revolt against a new ruler. But its language is too large for any ordinary Israelite king: the Lord’s anointed is called God’s Son and given the nations as his inheritance. The New Testament sees its fulfillment in Jesus. Early Christians prayed it in Acts 4 when persecuted. Revelation draws on it repeatedly (2:26-27; 11:15-18; 12:5; 19:15), so it is one of the keys to the book.
observation: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” (v. 1).
“The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his anointed” (v. 2).
“He who sits in the heavens laughs” (v. 4).
“As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (v. 6).
“You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (v. 7).
“Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession” (v. 8).
“Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (v. 11).
“Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (v. 12).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a question of astonishment: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” It is a futile revolt. “The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his anointed, saying, Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us.” They think of God’s rule as a prison. The picture is one of the whole world, with its political powers, in rebellion against God and his Messiah. This is exactly the setting of Revelation: the dragon, the beasts, and the kings of the earth raging against the Lamb.

Then God’s response: “He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision.” It is not a happy laugh but the laughter of one who sees that the attempt is hopeless. Then he speaks to them in his wrath: “As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill.” The rebels cannot undo what God has done.

The King himself speaks next: “I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” This is the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:14) and finds its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus, whom the New Testament declares to be the Son at his baptism, transfiguration, and resurrection (Acts 13:33; Romans 1:4; Hebrews 1:5). “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.” Revelation takes this promise and applies it to Christ and to those who share his rule (2:26-27; 12:5; 19:15). This does not mean we have violent power; it means that his kingdom will conquer all that opposes it.

Finally, a warning with an invitation: “Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth. Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him.” To kiss the Son is to submit to him and to honor him. The psalm began with the first Psalm’s word for the blessed man and ends with the same word for all who take refuge in the Son. There is a way out of judgment: take refuge in him. The same Son who will judge the nations invites us into his shelter. And so the great conflict of Revelation is not a conflict between equal powers: it is between a rebellious world and the King whom God has installed.
connection: 2 Samuel 7:12-16 is the promise to David. Acts 4:23-31 quotes the psalm in prayer. Acts 13:32-33, Hebrews 1:5, and 5:5 quote verse 7. Matthew 3:17 and 17:5 echo it at Jesus’ baptism and transfiguration. Revelation 2:26-27, 11:15-18, 12:5, 19:15 draw on it. Philippians 2:9-11 describes the nations bowing to Jesus. Ephesians 1:20-22 speaks of his rule. Psalm 110:1-2 speaks of his enemies as his footstool. Psalm 1:1 and 2:12 frame the opening of the Psalter with “blessed.” John 3:36 warns about the Son’s wrath.
application:
When news about the nations is discouraging, say verse 4 to yourself. God is not anxious.

Take refuge in the Son today by naming something you fear and entrusting it to Christ.

Pray for rulers by name, that they would kiss the Son and be wise.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what raging and plotting you see.
Thank him for the Son he has set on Zion.
